reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Second most common urea cycle disorder, caused by biallelic ASL variants (argininosuccinate lyase deficiency)
Neonatal-onset form presents with hyperammonaemic encephalopathy: poor feeding, vomiting, tachypnoea, lethargy and coma in the first days of life
Biochemical hallmark is markedly raised plasma and urine argininosuccinic acid, with raised citrulline and low arginine
Late-onset disease may present with episodic hyperammonaemia, developmental delay, learning difficulties or chronic liver involvement
Distinctive features include trichorrhexis nodosa (brittle, fragile hair) and a tendency to hepatomegaly and hepatic fibrosis
Systemic hypertension and neurocognitive impairment can occur even with good ammonia control, reflecting nitric oxide deficiency
Confirm with plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid, enzyme assay in fibroblasts/red cells and ASL sequencing
Management combines protein restriction, arginine supplementation and nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate/phenylbutyrate), with haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Argininosuccinic aciduria is caused by deficiency of argininosuccinate lyase, the urea cycle enzyme that cleaves argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. The block prevents completion of ureagenesis, so waste nitrogen cannot be efficiently converted to urea and ammonia accumulates. Argininosuccinate itself builds up to high levels in blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, while arginine (a downstream product) becomes deficient. Because arginine is also the substrate for nitric oxide synthesis, chronic arginine deficiency and argininosuccinate accumulation are thought to contribute to the hypertension, hepatic disease and neurocognitive problems that can persist despite adequate ammonia control, distinguishing this disorder from other urea cycle defects. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Other urea cycle disorders (OTC deficiency, citrullinaemia type 1, CPS1 and NAGS deficiency)
Fatty acid oxidation disorders with hyperammonaemia
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids showing raised argininosuccinate and citrulline with low arginine
Blood gas to assess for respiratory alkalosis of hyperammonaemia
ASL gene sequencing or enzyme assay in erythrocytes/fibroblasts
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging/elastography for fibrosis
Blood pressure monitoring for systemic hypertension
redFlags: Neonatal hyperammonaemic coma requiring emergency ammonia removal
Rapidly rising ammonia with encephalopathy at any age
reference.prognosis: Early recognition and prompt control of hyperammonaemia improve survival, but neurocognitive impairment, hypertension and hepatic disease may develop even with satisfactory metabolic control, so outcome is more variable than in some other urea cycle disorders.
pitfalls: Delaying ammonia measurement and treatment in an encephalopathic neonate
Assuming normal ammonia control prevents all complications, missing hypertension and liver disease
Overlooking argininosuccinate on amino acid analysis and misclassifying the urea cycle defect
Neglecting arginine supplementation, which is required to correct the downstream deficiency
Failing to prepare an emergency regimen for catabolic illness or surgery
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Saudubray, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Institute a protein-restricted diet with arginine supplementation, as the enzyme block leaves arginine deficient, to support residual ureagenesis
Give nitrogen-scavenger therapy with sodium benzoate or sodium phenylbutyrate to remove waste nitrogen

Manage hyperammonaemic crises by stopping protein, giving high-calorie glucose and lipid to halt catabolism, intravenous arginine and scavengers, and haemodialysis or haemofiltration for severe or refractory hyperammonaemia
Monitor and manage complications that persist despite ammonia control, particularly systemic hypertension and hepatic fibrosis with liver function tests and elastography
Undertake regular biochemical monitoring of ammonia, plasma amino acids and nutritional status with neurodevelopmental follow-up
Coordinate care with a metabolic dietitian and specialist metabolic team and consider liver transplantation in severe disease
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive ASL inheritance
